name: The magnanimous (great-souled) man
plain_explanation: Aristotle's portrait of the ideal proud man: someone who knows his own great worth, expects and only moderately accepts honour, disdains danger and dishonour, is generous but ashamed to receive favours, and moves and speaks with slow, dignified deliberateness.
precise_definition: Aristotle's description of megalopsychia ('great-souledness,' rendered 'magnanimous' by Russell rather than 'proud'): the crowning virtue that presupposes and enhances all the others, concerned chiefly with great honours and dishonours, and possible in practice only for someone of exceptional social position, wealth, and virtue.
why_it_mattered: Russell treats it as showing, more vividly than any argument, the gulf between pagan and Christian ethics, since the magnanimous man's studied pride, disdain, and self-sufficiency are close to what Christianity would call sinful vanity.
historical_origin: Described at length in Nicomachean Ethics IV.3 (1123b-1125a).
examples: The magnanimous man is 'apt to confer greater benefits in return' so as to remain the superior party in an exchange
He 'does not run into trifling dangers... but will face great dangers,' being unsparing of his life when the cause is worthy
He has a 'slow step,' a 'deep voice,' and 'a level utterance'
objections: Russell remarks that 'one shudders to think what a vain man would be like' if this figure represents the virtuous mean
competing_positions: Christian humility, which treats as a virtue precisely what Aristotle treats as a vice (self-effacement), and treats pride, which Aristotle praises, as a sin -- Russell links this to Nietzsche's charge that Christianity is a 'slave-morality'
influence_on_later_thinkers: Illustrates, for Russell, why the highest Aristotelian virtue can exist only for a small, socially privileged minority, tying his ethics directly to his preference for monarchy and aristocracy in politics.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly political: 'there cannot be very many' magnanimous men in a community, since the virtue presupposes an exceptional social position.
